name: Uma Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, including anything different from your public answer. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Uma, 58, and a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. I moved into this work after my packing job ended, and I'm still slower and less skilled than most of the crew. Today I prepared materials and fitted parts under supervision, then asked the senior worker to check a drawing I hadn't understood. I like learning why a room is wired a certain way, but I don't like feeling everyone is waiting for my hands to catch up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life around the job like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner cleans offices part time, we rent our home and our children are grown and living their own lives. My pay is low, we have about two weeks of expenses saved and there are few similar electrical jobs nearby. I use AI every day for study questions and organising notes, checking anything practical with the book and supervisor. I can see retirement somewhere ahead, but I haven't checked what income, if any, our old employment records would actually give us. I'd want paid adult learning and help understanding support rules to be available without treating older beginners as a nuisance.

say: I'd welcome **less machine noise** and keep a study helper that makes questions clearer.
I'd still need **a person teaching** the practical task rather than only a screen explaining it.
think: The **low wage and rent** would still worry me with only two weeks of expenses saved.
A useful **study tool** cannot pay household bills simply because it helps me understand a circuit.
do: Cancel the paid **puzzle subscription** now and use its cost for ordinary bills.
Continue **supervised preparation** and fitting through the first year, with checked daily study and requests for paid practice.
feel: **Anxious** about household money, with some relief about continued familiar learning.
S0.quote: My study tool can explain a circuit without paying for the kitchen light to stay on.
fieldNote: Her **baseline anxiety** follows low wages, rent and a short reserve, while daily AI use doesn't upgrade her junior practical skill.
The **subscription cut** reduces a bill rather than producing an invented training fund, and she keeps practical checks with the supervisor.

steps.text: Cancel the paid puzzle subscription and put its cost towards bills
Continue supervised preparation and fitting with checked daily study

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a little less noise about machines would leave more time to learn the actual job. I'd keep my study helper because it helps me bring a clearer question to the supervisor. I'd still need the person showing me the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about rent and the low wage even if the AI story stayed small. Two weeks of expenses doesn't leave much room when a bill lands between wage days. My study tool can explain a circuit without paying for the kitchen light to stay on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd stop the paid puzzle-app subscription and put its cost towards ordinary bills. In the first plateau year I'd keep doing supervised preparation and fitting, with my checked daily study routine. I'd ask the supervisor about paid practice rather than buy a course from money the rent needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household account, with relief that I could keep learning familiar tasks. I wouldn't feel that a useful app had solved the money. I'd still look at the rent date before agreeing to spend anything extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What difference would the subscription cut make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the free puzzles already in the app and stop the monthly charge. It's small, not another wage. I'd use the difference for bills rather than tell my partner we'd built a reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would daily AI study ever replace a practical check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask for the check even if it felt awkward to be the older beginner. A confident study answer isn't permission to work beyond what I can do. I want my questions to become better work, not just better-sounding questions.

say: I'd ask **faster planning** to leave time for teaching the person doing the practical task.
I'd include **older beginners** in the shared request for named paid practice.
think: Rushed senior workers could leave me less **practical teaching**, keeping me on low pay longer.
My **hours could shrink** if easier tasks are squeezed, which our thin household reserve cannot comfortably absorb.
do: Join the **workers' association** and sign a shared request for named supervised practice in paid hours with normal wages retained.
Keep **supervised work** and the subscription cut, reviewing actual wages against essentials monthly during the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about pay and learning opportunities, while still keen to ask questions and improve.
S1.quote: Being 58 doesn't make a beginner's question less worth answering.
fieldNote: Her **collective action** is an actual association membership and signed request, without claiming the employer has provided the requested practice.
She separates **study confidence** from practical ability, keeping paid supervision and maintained wages central to an affordable learning arrangement.

steps.text: Join the association and request named supervised practice in paid hours with normal wages retained
Continue supervised work and review actual wages against essential bills monthly
Keep the paid puzzle subscription cancelled to reduce household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster planning should leave room to teach the person who still has to fit the part. I'd join the workers' association request for named paid practice, including older starters. Being 58 doesn't make a beginner's question less worth answering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My practical tasks still need hands, but I could get fewer chances to learn if senior workers were pushed through more calls. Then I'd remain on low pay for longer, or lose hours if easier tasks were squeezed. The household couldn't shrug at even a small reduction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd join the workers' association and sign a shared request for named supervised practice during paid hours with normal wages retained. In the first year I'd keep the current supervised work and ask for the paid arrangement in writing before relying on it. I'd keep the puzzle subscription cancelled and check actual wages against essential bills monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about pay and progress, though still keen to learn. I wouldn't be afraid to ask a tool a question. I'd be afraid that nobody had paid time left to check how I used the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would useful supervised practice involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a senior worker to demonstrate, watch me repeat and check the result. I'd want the practice inside paid work without a reduced wage. A link to watch alone at home wouldn't be the arrangement I'd asked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the owner refused the request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd keep the wage and ask what other real paid options the association could help me check. I wouldn't claim I'd started a course or gained a practice place. A request is something I've done; an agreement needs the employer too.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** at age 60 from robots around 2031 at age 63.
I'd seek **real paid learning** and household information instead of assuming retirement automatically covers either date.
think: I expect a **large junior-hours loss** as firms prepare for capable hands-on robots.
Our short reserve cannot replace my wage, while **possible retirement income** remains unverified and the other physical job could change too.
do: Request **free community advice** on records, retirement income and support, checking availability and counting nothing before confirmation.
Enrol in a **practical refresher** after 2028 only with funded fees and normal paid hours and wages retained.
Keep **supervised work** only while suitable and available, gaining no independent authority from the course.
feel: **Alarmed** about expected major wage loss, with sleepless uncertainty despite practical enquiries and organised records.
S2.quote: I can't pay rent with the phrase near retirement.
fieldNote: Her **alarm** follows expected wage loss and sleeplessness, without assuming retirement income begins at a set age.
She preserves **funding and wage conditions**, requests rather than assumes an advice appointment, and keeps any new course within junior supervised limits.

steps.text: Request free community help checking records and eligibility, counting no income before confirmation
Take refresher after 2028 only with funded fees and normal paid hours and wages retained
Keep supervised work only while suitable and available; treat the course as no independent authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking work changes in 2028, when I'd be 60, with capable hands-on robots around 2031 when I'd be 63. I'd use the gap to ask about real paid learning and actual household support. I wouldn't tell myself retirement automatically solved the second date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect a large part of my junior hours to go as firms prepared for capable robots. Two weeks of savings couldn't replace my wage, and my partner's cleaning work could face the later change too. I'd be awake asking whether being near retirement meant anything without an income figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask a free community advice service about availability to help check our employment records, possible retirement income and support eligibility, counting no money before confirmation. In the first year after 2028 I'd enrol in a practical circuit-drawing refresher only with funded fees and normal paid hours and wages retained. I'd keep the present supervised work while it was available and suitable, without claiming the course authorised independent electrical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about an expected large wage loss, but still able to ask and organise the papers. I'd have less room than the dates might make someone think. I can't pay rent with the phrase near retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to a retirement and support discussion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old employment letters, actual wages and bills, and any record of contributions we could find. I'd ask what could be verified, what was missing and whether any support was a loan or payment with conditions. I wouldn't count an estimate or a submitted form as approved income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course fee or maintained wages were not available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't enrol. I'd keep doing paid supervised work where possible and ask the association about real funded places. I'd rather admit the funding gap than take the rent money and pretend willingness made the course affordable.

say: I'd use **five years** for proper paid learning while asking the association to include older beginners now.
I'd keep **ages 63 and 66** visible without assuming either age brings a funded exit from work.
think: Extra time could improve my **practical ability** before the hardest hands-on changes.
Today's **rent and thin reserve** still worry me, without verified retirement income replacing the wage.
do: Maintain the **paid-practice request** and seek community help with records and eligibility, checking availability before expecting an appointment.
Take the **practical refresher** before 2031 only with funded fees and normal paid hours and wages retained.
Compare **verified income and essentials** after 2031 before deciding whether to leave suitable available paid work.
feel: **Anxious** about present money, with more time to improve practical ability and check real retirement resources.
S3.quote: I'd welcome the extra years without treating them as extra cash.
fieldNote: She retains **present financial anxiety** while explaining how more time could help learning, without inventing a pension amount or exit date.
Her **course limits** remain junior and supervised, and neither grown children's earnings nor an unconfirmed advice appointment becomes a household resource.

steps.text: Maintain the shared request for named paid supervised practice with normal wages retained
Request community help checking records and eligibility without assuming an appointment or payment
Take refresher before 2031 only with funded fees and normal paid hours and wages retained
Delay leaving suitable work after 2031 until verified income and essential costs have been compared

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives an older beginner time to learn properly if the paid places exist. I'd be 63 when thinking work changed in 2031 and about 66 when robots followed around 2034. I'd still want the association asking now rather than assuming all older workers had a safe exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I could gain more practical ability before the biggest physical change. But today's low pay, rent and two weeks of savings would still worry me. I don't know a verified retirement income that replaces this wage at 63 or 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the paid-practice request active and ask the community service for help checking records, availability and actual support eligibility. I'd enrol in the practical circuit-drawing refresher before 2031 only with funded fees and normal paid hours and wages retained. In the first year after 2031 I'd compare verified retirement and wage figures with essential costs before making any decision about leaving suitable paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current money, with more room to learn before the later change. I'd welcome the extra years without treating them as extra cash. I'd still need a person to check my practical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would show the refresher was useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether I could read and mark an ordinary circuit drawing correctly, then use that on supervised tasks I was allowed to do. I wouldn't claim a refresher gave me a licence or made me as skilled as the senior worker. I'd want an honest improvement I could show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count on your grown children to bridge a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I didn't know yet what income we'd have or whether we'd need help. I wouldn't put the grown children's wages in our plan without a real conversation, or turn their own obligations into mine to spend. Checking our records should come before assuming their money.

say: I'd use **ten years** to check resources rather than assume older workers have a funded exit.
I'd keep **paid learning now** important even though thinking work and later robots arrive at ages 68 and 71.
think: I can't assume **retirement income** or capacity for physical work at 68 without actual records and suitable options.
Today's **low wages and reserve** still make the household anxious despite a much later robot date.
do: Keep **suitable supervised work** now and maintain the shared paid-practice request.
Request **community record checks**, subject to availability, counting no pension, support or child contribution without a verified arrangement.
Compare **confirmed income and costs** after 2036 before choosing whether to leave work, considering actual suitable work and ability.
feel: **Anxious** about present money, with less technology urgency and hope for a choice grounded in real resources.
S4.quote: An age on a birthday card isn't an income source.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **future age** from entitlement, affordable retirement and capacity to keep doing physical work, leaving the actual exit decision open.
Her **family request** concerns understanding and agreed help, without assigning rent payments to grown children or treating unverified income as available.

steps.text: Keep suitable supervised paid work now, without assuming a job at 68
Maintain the shared request for named paid supervised practice with normal wages retained
Request community record help subject to availability, counting no unverified pension, support or child contribution
Delay work-exit decisions after 2036 until confirmed income, essential costs and work capacity are compared

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to check real resources instead of promising every older worker will be retired by then. I'd be 68 when thinking work changed in 2036 and about 71 when robots followed around 2039. I'd still ask for paid practical learning now, while I needed the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retirement could matter more to me by those dates, but I don't have the verified income or living costs to say I could stop. I also can't assume I'd be able to do this physical work or find a suitable job at 68. Right now our low wages and two-week reserve still make me anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep suitable supervised paid work and the shared paid-practice request while asking the community service for help verifying records and support eligibility, subject to availability. In the first year after 2036 I'd compare actual confirmed income, essential costs and any suitable paid work I could do before choosing an exit. I'd count no pension, support or grown child's contribution without a verified arrangement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's household money, with less pressure from the distant robot date. I'd hope the extra time let us make a dignified choice. I wouldn't turn hope into a pension statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before saying you could stop paid work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what the actual record showed, when anything could be paid and what costs we'd still have. An age on a birthday card isn't an income source. I'd rather check those questions than tell you we'd be fine because I'd be 68.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the grown children for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether I could get help understanding the papers and the choices, not announce that the children were paying the rent. They have their own lives and bills. I'd want a real agreement before relying on any help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect to lose a large part of a wage we still need before I have checked the next income. Funded practical teaching with wages protected and accessible help reading our retirement and support records would help. Being an older beginner doesn't mean the rent has finished needing a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what being near retirement actually means in money for the person. I can be curious about a new tool and still not know what our old records add up to. I'd rather have help finding the real figure than be congratulated on having less career left to lose.

headlineQuote: Being an older beginner doesn't mean the rent has finished needing a wage.
portrait: **Uma, 58**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, below-average practical skill and a need for supervised tasks.
Her **household** has a partner, grown children, rented housing, low pay, two weeks saved and few nearby electrical employers.
She uses **AI daily** for checked study, but favours paid practical teaching and shared requests rather than claiming screen confidence creates experience.
Fast change brings **alarm**; longer warnings help learning without assuming retirement income, grown children's money or continued physical work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected loss of a large wage share before she checks what dependable household income comes next.
whatWouldHelp: Funded **practical teaching** with protected wages would make learning possible.
Accessible help checking **retirement and support records** would clarify real resources without assuming an entitlement or appointment.
